title: From graphics pipelines to GPGPU
text:
CHAPTER 15. GPUS AND THE COMPUTE REVOLUTION
SECTION 15.1. FROM GRAPHICS PIPELINES TO GPGPU

The deep learning revolution of the 2010s was made possible as much by hardware as by algorithms. Backpropagation was known since the 1980s (Chapter 13); what changed was that a chip designed to draw video game graphics turned out to be very good at the arithmetic neural networks need: huge numbers of multiply-add operations on arrays. This section explains what a graphics pipeline does, why it demands massive parallelism, how graphics processors became programmable, and how researchers in the early 2000s bent them to general-purpose computing (GPGPU) before purpose-built tools existed. Section 15.2 covers CUDA, the parallel programming model, and how training is spread across many GPUs.

1. What 3D graphics requires

To display a 3D scene, a computer must, for every frame (30 to 60 or more frames per second):

  - Transform every vertex of every triangle from model coordinates to screen coordinates: a 4 x 4 matrix multiplication per vertex in homogeneous coordinates,

        [x' y' z' w']^T = M_projection * M_view * M_model * [x y z 1]^T

    followed by division by w' for perspective.
  - Compute lighting at vertices or pixels: dot products of surface normals with light directions, for example diffuse intensity = max(0, n . l).
  - Rasterize: determine which screen pixels each triangle covers.
  - Shade each pixel (fragment): look up textures (images wrapped on surfaces), interpolate colors, combine lighting.
  - Resolve visibility with a depth buffer (z-buffer): keep the nearest fragment per pixel.

A 1920 x 1080 display has about 2 million pixels. At 60 frames per second and with several fragments per pixel and dozens of operations per fragment, that is billions of operations per second, nearly all of them independent of each other: each vertex and each pixel can be processed separately. This is "embarrassingly parallel" work, and it is dominated by small matrix and vector arithmetic in floating point.

2. The fixed-function era

Early 3D accelerators for PCs in the mid-to-late 1990s (from companies such as 3dfx, Nvidia, ATI and others) implemented rasterization and texturing in fixed-function hardware: circuits that did one job, configured by a few settings. The CPU still did geometry transformation and lighting.

Nvidia's GeForce 256, announced on 31 August 1999 and released in October 1999, moved transform and lighting (T&L) onto the graphics chip as well. Nvidia marketed it as "the world's first GPU" (graphics processing unit). The term itself was older (Sony had used "GPU" for the PlayStation's graphics chip in 1994, and in the 1970s-80s it had other meanings; programmable graphics processors such as the Texas Instruments TMS34010 of 1986 also existed). But the GeForce 256 marks the point at which the whole 3D pipeline ran on a dedicated chip.

The pipeline was still fixed: developers could choose among built-in lighting and texturing modes but not write their own algorithms.

3. Programmable shaders

Game developers wanted custom effects: realistic materials, bump mapping, shadows, water. The answer was programmability. Microsoft's DirectX 8 (2000) and the GeForce 3 (2001), the first card with programmable pixel shaders, introduced small programs called shaders:

  - Vertex shaders: run once per vertex; transform positions and compute per-vertex values.
  - Pixel (fragment) shaders: run once per pixel fragment; compute its color from interpolated inputs and texture lookups.

Early shaders were very limited (short programs, few instructions, limited precision, no loops). Over the next few years they gained longer programs, flow control and, crucially, floating-point arithmetic throughout (around 2002-2003, with cards such as ATI's Radeon 9700 and Nvidia's GeForce FX series supporting floating-point pixel processing). High-level shading languages appeared: Nvidia's Cg, Microsoft's HLSL and the OpenGL Shading Language (GLSL).

A pixel shader is a function evaluated independently at millions of points in parallel, with inputs read from textures (2D arrays) and outputs written to an image. That is exactly a data-parallel computation on arrays.

4. The architecture difference: latency versus throughput

CPUs and GPUs are optimized for different goals.

A CPU core is designed to minimize latency for one thread: large caches (Section 6.4), branch prediction, out-of-order execution, deep pipelines. Most of its silicon area goes to control logic and cache, not arithmetic units.

A GPU is designed to maximize throughput over many threads:

  - Many simple arithmetic units, grouped so that many execute the same instruction on different data (SIMD, or Nvidia's SIMT, "single instruction, multiple threads").
  - Little control logic per arithmetic unit; branches that diverge within a group are executed serially, so uniform code runs best.
  - Small caches per unit; instead of avoiding memory latency, the GPU hides it by keeping thousands of threads in flight and switching to ready ones while others wait for memory (massive multithreading).
  - Very high memory bandwidth through wide memory buses and fast graphics memory (GDDR, later HBM).

An analogy: a CPU is a few expert workers who each finish a complex task very quickly; a GPU is thousands of workers who each do simple steps, slowly individually but enormous in total output, as long as the work can be divided.

Amdahl's law (Section 6.4) warns that the serial parts of a program limit the speedup from parallel hardware. Graphics, and as it turned out neural networks, have almost no serial part at the level of individual arithmetic operations.

5. Arithmetic intensity and the roofline

Whether a computation runs fast on a GPU depends on its arithmetic intensity I: floating-point operations per byte moved from memory. The roofline model states:

    attainable performance = min( peak FLOP rate, I * memory bandwidth )

Below a critical intensity (peak FLOPs divided by bandwidth), a computation is memory-bound; above it, compute-bound.

Examples:

  - Vector addition c = a + b: one addition per 12 bytes moved (two 4-byte reads, one write): I = 1/12 FLOP per byte. Memory-bound on any hardware.
  - Matrix-vector product y = A x with an n x n matrix: about 2n^2 FLOPs and n^2 * 4 bytes for A: I about 0.5. Memory-bound.
  - Matrix-matrix product C = A B with n x n matrices: 2n^3 FLOPs and about 3 n^2 * 4 bytes, so I is about n/6. For n = 1000, about 170 FLOPs per byte. Compute-bound if the data are reused well through on-chip memory (tiling).

Neural network training is dominated by matrix multiplications (fully connected layers, and convolutions rearranged as matrix multiplications), batched over many examples. Batching turns matrix-vector products into matrix-matrix products, raising arithmetic intensity so the GPU's arithmetic units stay busy. This is one reason minibatch training (Section 13.1) matters for hardware efficiency, not only for optimization.

6. GPGPU before CUDA

From about 2002 to 2006, researchers used graphics programming interfaces (OpenGL, DirectX) for non-graphics computation, a practice that became known as GPGPU (general-purpose computation on GPUs; Mark Harris, founder of the gpgpu.org community site, has said he coined the term). The trick was to disguise computation as rendering:

  - Store input arrays as textures (2D images of floating-point values).
  - Draw a rectangle covering exactly the output array's size in pixels, so that the pixel shader runs once per output element.
  - Write the computation in the pixel shader, reading inputs from textures.
  - Render into a texture ("render to texture") instead of the screen; that texture is the output, and can be the input of the next pass.

Matrix multiplication, for example, could be computed in multiple passes, each pixel accumulating part of a dot product. Researchers implemented linear algebra, fast Fourier transforms, fluid simulation, image processing, sorting, database operations and physical simulations this way. A 2001 Supercomputing conference paper by Scott Larsen and David McAllister on fast matrix multiplies using graphics hardware is one early example, and surveys around 2005-2007 (Owens, Luebke, Govindaraju, Harris, Krüger, Lefohn and Purcell) catalogued the field.

The difficulties were severe: programmers had to think in terms of textures, pixels and rendering passes; there was no general memory writes to arbitrary addresses (scatter); precision and rounding rules varied between vendors; debugging was painful; and data transfer between CPU and GPU was slow.

Stream programming languages hid some of this. BrookGPU, developed in the Stanford University graphics group (Ian Buck and colleagues), was a compiler and runtime for a stream programming language based on ANSI C: programmers wrote "kernels" applied to "streams" of data, and Brook generated the shader code. Its last major release was in 2004. In 2004 Nvidia hired Ian Buck and paired him with John Nickolls to develop a proper general-purpose programming platform for its GPUs, which became CUDA (Section 15.2).

7. Unified shaders and the G80

Through the mid-2000s, GPUs had separate vertex and pixel shader units. If a scene had many vertices and few pixels (or the reverse), some units sat idle. The unified shader model replaced them with a single pool of general processors that could run any kind of shader. Nvidia's G80 architecture, introduced with the GeForce 8800 GTX in November 2006, was Nvidia's first unified shader design, with 128 scalar "stream processors," and it was designed together with CUDA so that the same processors could be programmed directly for general computation. (ATI's Xenos chip for the Xbox 360, 2005, had used unified shaders earlier in a console.)

The G80 marks the transition from GPGPU as a hack to GPU computing as a platform. From then on, each generation added features for general computation: double precision, error-correcting memory for data centers, larger caches, faster interconnects, and eventually specialized matrix units (tensor cores, which Nvidia introduced with its Volta architecture in 2017).

8. First neural networks on GPUs

Neural network researchers noticed the opportunity early:

  - 2004: Kyoung-Su Oh and Keechul Jung published a GPU implementation of a neural network (a multilayer perceptron for text detection), using graphics shaders.
  - 2006: Kumar Chellapilla, Sidd Puri and Patrice Simard (Microsoft Research) described a GPU implementation of a convolutional neural network for document processing, reportedly about 4 times faster than an equivalent CPU implementation.
  - 2009: Rajat Raina, Anand Madhavan and Andrew Ng reported training large deep belief networks (with around 100 million parameters) using GPUs (GeForce GTX 280), with speedups of up to about 70 times over CPUs, in "Large-scale Deep Unsupervised Learning using Graphics Processors."
  - 2010-2012: Dan Ciresan, Ueli Meier, Luca Gambardella and Jürgen Schmidhuber trained deep multilayer perceptrons and CNNs on GPUs, winning several image recognition competitions in 2011 and 2012; and in 2012, AlexNet (Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Hinton) used two GeForce GTX 580 GPUs to win the ImageNet challenge (Chapter 16).

By then, CUDA had made writing such code far easier than the shader era allowed.

9. Lessons

  - Hardware built for a mass consumer market (games) provided cheap, enormous parallel compute that a niche field (neural networks) could exploit; economies of scale mattered, in contrast to the Lisp machine story (Section 11.2).
  - The algorithms that won were those that map well onto the hardware: dense, regular, data-parallel matrix arithmetic. This "hardware lottery" (a term popularized by Sara Hooker in 2020) shaped which ideas succeeded.
  - Arithmetic intensity, memory bandwidth and data movement, not raw FLOPs alone, determine real performance; the same is true for embedded inference on a microcontroller or edge accelerator.

10. Summary

  - 3D graphics requires billions of independent floating-point vector and matrix operations per second on vertices and pixels.
  - The GeForce 256 (1999) put transform and lighting on the graphics chip and was marketed as the first GPU; programmable shaders arrived with DirectX 8 and the GeForce 3 (2001), with floating-point pixel processing around 2002-2003.
  - GPUs optimize throughput with many SIMD/SIMT arithmetic units, massive multithreading to hide memory latency, and high memory bandwidth; CPUs optimize single-thread latency.
  - The roofline model: performance = min(peak FLOPs, arithmetic intensity * bandwidth); matrix multiplication has high intensity, so it suits GPUs; batching raises intensity.
  - GPGPU (about 2002-2006) disguised computation as rendering with textures and pixel shaders; BrookGPU at Stanford abstracted it; Nvidia hired Ian Buck in 2004 to build CUDA.
  - The G80 (GeForce 8800, November 2006) brought unified shaders designed for general computing; early neural network GPU work (2004, 2006, 2009) led to the 2012 breakthroughs.
